16ec985cfff3fbd7.text: What makes instructions work. Instructions are a text type with one job: help someone do something right, the first time. Good ones share the same features. A clear title. Say what you'll make or do: How to make a cheese toastie. What you need. List the materials and tools before the steps, so nobody gets halfway and stops. Numbered steps in order. One action per step. If the order matters (and it usually does), the numbers show it. Start with a doing word. Cut, spread, press, wait. It tells the reader exactly what to do. Be precise. Two slices beats some bread. For 3 minutes beats for a bit. Pictures and warnings. A photo or diagram can save a hundred words. A warning (Careful: hot!) keeps people safe. The secret? Test it. Give your instructions to someone who has never done the task. Watch, and don't help. Every time they get stuck, you've found a step to fix.

cc7b524f2a745a84.text: The Exact Instructions Challenge. In 2017, a YouTuber called Josh Darnit posted a video that went viral. His two kids had to write instructions for making a peanut butter and jam sandwich. Josh would then follow them exactly — doing only what the words said. It went badly. When the instructions said to put peanut butter on the bread, he put the whole jar on the bread. When they said to spread it, he used his hand. The kids rewrote their instructions again and again, getting more and more frustrated. It looks like a joke, but teachers around the world use the same challenge. It shows something real: you know a task so well that you skip steps. Your reader can't read your mind. Think about it. Why did the kids' instructions fail? What does this show about writing for someone else? How could they have tested their steps sooner?

d59690088506a3be.text: What makes instructions work. Instructions (or procedures) are a text type designed for one purpose: to get a reader to complete a task correctly, first time, without help. Effective instructions share recognisable features. A specific title that names the outcome: How to make a cheese toastie. Materials and equipment listed up front, so the reader can prepare. Numbered, sequential steps, each containing a single action. Imperative verbs (commands) at the start of each step: cut, spread, press. Precise language: quantities, times and positions, so nothing is left to guess. Visuals and warnings, which often communicate faster and more safely than words. Writers rarely get instructions right in one go, because they know the task too well and skip “obvious” steps. That's why professionals test them on real users: watch silently, note every hesitation, and revise.

7f73e8f59172ee8f.text: The Exact Instructions Challenge. In 2017, YouTuber Josh Darnit posted a video that spread fast online. His two children wrote instructions for making a peanut butter and jam sandwich. He then followed them exactly, doing only what the words said. The results were chaos. “Put peanut butter on the bread” got the whole jar placed on a slice. “Spread it” was done with his hand. The kids rewrote their steps again and again, and got more and more frustrated. The “exact instructions” challenge is now a common classroom activity. It shows a real problem in writing for an audience. When you know a task well, you skip steps that seem obvious to you. They are not obvious to your reader. Think about it. Why did the kids' instructions fail? What does this show about writing for someone else? How could they have tested their steps sooner?
